'''Jeremy Adam Kahn''' (born October 26, 1969) is an American mathematician. He works on [[hyperbolic geometry]], [[Riemann surface]]s and [[complex dynamics]].

==Education==
Kahn grew up in [[New York City]] and attended [[Hunter College High School]]. He was a [[child prodigy]] who mastered [[quadratic equations]] at the age of 7, at the age of 8 designed an equation identical to the one [[Carl Gauss]] designed at the age of 9, and proved the Pythagorean Theorem at the age of 10.<ref name="csm">{{cite web|first=Robert|last= Marquand |url=https://www.csmonitor.com/1985/0712/dkahn-f.html|title=Growing up gifted: three-time math Olympian Jeremy Kahn|newspaper=[[The Christian Science Monitor]]|date=July 12, 1985}}</ref> Kahn was part of the [[Johns Hopkins University]] [[Study of Mathematically Precocious Youth]] longitudinal cohort. At the age of 11, he scored a 780 out of a possible 800 on the math portion of the [[SAT-I]] exam.<ref name=csm /> At the age of 13, he became the youngest person ever to make the United States [[International Mathematical Olympiad]] team <ref>{{cite journal
 | last = Stanley | first = Julian
 | date = March 1987
 | doi = 10.1177/107621758701000208
 | issue = 2
 | journal = Gifted Child Today
 | pages = 22–23
 | title = Making the IMO Team: The Power of Early Identification and Encouragement
 | url = https://gwern.net/doc/iq/high/smpy/1987-stanley.pdf
 | volume = 10}}</ref> He participated in the Olympiad four times, winning silver medals in 1983 and 1984, and gold medals in 1985 and 1986.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.imo-official.org/participant_r.aspx?id=1411|title = International Mathematical Olympiad}}</ref>

On the basis of his success in the [[Putnam competition]], he became a Putnam Fellow in 1988.<ref>{{Cite journal|url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/2324716|jstor = 2324716|last1 = Klosinski|first1 = Leonard F.|last2 = Alexanderson|first2 = G. L.|last3 = Larson|first3 = Loren C.|title = The William Lowell Putnam Mathematical Competition|journal = The American Mathematical Monthly|year = 1989|volume = 96|issue = 8|pages = 688–695|doi = 10.1080/00029890.1989.11972264}}</ref> He received a bachelor's degree in mathematics at [[Harvard University]], then received his Ph.D. from the [[University of California, Berkeley]] in 1995 under [[Curtis McMullen]] with the thesis ''Holomorphic removability of quadratic polynomial Julia sets''.<ref>{{MathGenealogy|id=32225}}</ref>

==Career==
Kahn was assistant professor at the [[California Institute of Technology]] from 1995 to 1998 and was later a postdoc at the [[University of Toronto]]. After that, he worked for the investment firm [[Highbridge Capital Management]] as an analyst in [[financial mathematics]]. He was a postdoc and later assistant professor at the [[Stony Brook University]]. He is currently a professor of mathematics at [[Brown University]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://directory.brown.edu/uuid/0489ffd0-c072-523e-f868-d9830b179f36|title = Directory Page for &#124; Brown University}}</ref>

In 2012, Kahn and [[Vladimir Markovic]] received the [[Clay Research Award]] for their research on [[hyperbolic geometry]], specifically, for their result on immersions into a closed hyperbolic 3-manifold (proof of the [[surface subgroup conjecture]])<ref>{{cite arXiv|author=Kahn, J.|author2=Markovic, V.|eprint=0910.5501|title=Immersing almost geodesic surfaces in a closed hyperbolic 3-manifold|year=2009|class=math.GT}} Preprint in 2009; published in [[Annals of Mathematics]] in 2011</ref> and for their proof of the [[Ehrenpreis conjecture]].<ref>{{cite arXiv|author=Kahn, J.|author2=Markovic, V.|title=The good pants homology and a proof of the Ehrenpreis conjecture|year=2011|class=math.GT|eprint=1101.1330}}</ref>

In 2014 he was an [[invited speaker at the International Congress of Mathematicians]] in [[Seoul]] and gave a talk called "The Surface Subgroup and the Ehrenpreis Conjectures".
